Main.sentence: The Atlantic Ocean is the second largest of the world's five ___E:oceanic divisions U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borders_of_the_oceans)___ , with an area of about 85,133,000 km 2 (32,870,000 sq mi).

It covers approximately 17% of ___E:Earth's surface U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth#Surface)___ and about 24% of its water surface area. During the ___E:Age of Discovery U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_Discovery)___ , it was known for separating the ___E:New World U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_World)___ of the ___E:Americas U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Americas)___ ( ___E:North America U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_America)___ and ___E:South America U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_America)___ ) from the ___E:Old World U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_World)___ of ___E:Afro-Eurasia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afro-Eurasia)___ ( ___E:Africa U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africa)___ , ___E:Asia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asia)___ , and ___E:Europe U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europe)___ ).
Through its separation of Afro-Eurasia from the Americas, the Atlantic Ocean has played a central role in the development of human society, globalization, and the histories of many nations.

While the ___E:Norse U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norse_colonization_of_North_America)___ were the first known humans to cross the Atlantic, it was the ___E:expedition of Christopher Columbus U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_of_Christopher_Columbus)___ in 1492 that proved to be the most consequential.

Columbus's expedition ushered in an ___E:age of exploration U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_Discovery)___ and ___E:colonization of the Americas by European powers U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonization_of_the_Americas_by_European_powers)___ , most notably ___E:Portugal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_Empire)___ , ___E:Spain U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Empire)___ , ___E:France U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_colonial_empire)___ , and the ___E:United Kingdom U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Empire)___ .

From the 16th to 19th centuries, the Atlantic Ocean was the center of both ___E:an eponymous slave trade U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_slave_trade)___ and the ___E:Columbian exchange U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbian_exchange)___ while occasionally hosting naval battles.

Such naval battles, as well as growing trade from regional American powers like the United States and ___E:Brazil U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil)___ , both increased in degree during the early 20th century.

After ___E:World War II U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II)___ , major military operations became rarer, though notable postwar conflicts include the ___E:Cuban Missile Crisis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuban_Missile_Crisis)___ and the ___E:Falklands War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falklands_War)___ .
The ocean remains a core component of trade around the world.
The Atlantic Ocean's temperatures vary by location.
For example, the South Atlantic maintains warm temperatures year-round, as its basin countries are tropical.
The North Atlantic maintains a temperate climate, as its basin countries are temperate and have seasons of extremely low temperatures and high temperatures.

The Atlantic Ocean occupies an elongated, S-shaped basin extending longitudinally between Europe and Africa to the east, and the Americas to the west. As one component of the interconnected ___E:World Ocean U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Ocean)___ , it is connected in the north to the ___E:Arctic Ocean U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arctic_Ocean)___ , to the ___E:Pacific Ocean U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Ocean)___ in the southwest, the ___E:Indian Ocean U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Ocean)___ in the southeast, and the ___E:Southern Ocean U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Ocean)___ in the south.
Other definitions describe the Atlantic as extending southward to ___E:Antarctica U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antarctica)___ .
The Atlantic Ocean is divided in two parts, the northern and southern Atlantic, by the ___E:Equator U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equator)___ .
The oldest known mentions of an "Atlantic" sea come from ___E:Stesichorus U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stesichorus)___ around mid-sixth century BC (Sch. A.

R. 1. 211):  Atlantikôi pelágei (Ancient Greek: Ἀτλαντικῷ πελάγει , ' the Atlantic sea ' , etym . ' Sea of Atlas ' ) and in The Histories of ___E:Herodotus U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herodotus)___ around 450 BC (Hdt. 1.202.4): Atlantis thalassa (Ancient Greek: Ἀτλαντὶς θάλασσα , ' Sea of Atlas ' or ' the Atlantic sea '  ) where the name refers to "the sea beyond the ___E:pillars of Hercules U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pillars_of_Hercules)___ " which is said to be part of the sea that surrounds all land.  In these uses, the name refers to ___E:Atlas U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_(mythology))___ , the ___E:Titan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titan_(mythology))___ in ___E:Greek mythology U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_mythology)___ , who supported the heavens and who later appeared as a frontispiece in medieval maps and also lent his name to modern ___E:atlases U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_(geography))___ .

On the other hand, to early ___E:Greek U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Greece)___ sailors and in ancient Greek mythological literature such as the Iliad and the Odyssey , this all-encompassing ocean was instead known as ___E:Oceanus U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oceanus)___ , the gigantic river that encircled the world; in contrast to the enclosed seas well known to the Greeks: the Mediterranean and the Black Sea.  In contrast, the term "Atlantic" originally referred specifically to the ___E:Atlas Mountains U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Mountains)___ in Morocco and the sea off the ___E:Strait of Gibraltar U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strait_of_Gibraltar)___ and the West African coast.
The term " Aethiopian Ocean ", derived from ___E:Ancient Ethiopia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aethiopia)___ , was applied to the southern Atlantic as late as the mid-19th century.
During the ___E:Age of Discovery U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_Discovery)___ , the Atlantic was also known to English cartographers as the Great Western Ocean .

The pond is a term often used by British and American speakers in reference to the northern Atlantic Ocean, as a form of ___E:meiosis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meiosis_(figure_of_speech))___ , or ironic understatement.
It is used mostly when referring to events or circumstances "on this side of the pond" or "on the other side of the pond" or "across the pond", rather than to discuss the ocean itself.

The term dates to 1640, first appearing in print in a pamphlet released during the reign of ___E:Charles I U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_I_of_England)___ , and reproduced in 1869 in ___E:Nehemiah Wallington U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nehemiah_Wallington)___ 's Historical Notices of Events Occurring Chiefly in The Reign of Charles I , where "great Pond" is used in reference to the Atlantic Ocean by ___E:Francis Windebank U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Windebank)___ , Charles I's ___E:Secretary of State U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_of_State_(England))___ .

The ___E:International Hydrographic Organization U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Hydrographic_Organization)___ (IHO) defined the limits of the oceans and seas in 1953,  but some of these definitions have been revised since then and some are not recognized by various authorities, institutions, and countries, for example the ___E:CIA World Factbook U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CIA_World_Factbook)___ .
Correspondingly, the extent and number of oceans and seas vary.
The Atlantic Ocean is bounded on the west by North and South America.

It connects to the Arctic Ocean through the ___E:Labrador Sea U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labrador_Sea)___ , ___E:Denmark Strait U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark_Strait)___ , ___E:Greenland Sea U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenland_Sea)___ , ___E:Norwegian Sea U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norwegian_Sea)___ and ___E:Barents Sea U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barents_Sea)___ with the northern divider passing through ___E:Iceland U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland)___ and ___E:Svalbard U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Svalbard)___ .

To the east, the boundaries of the ocean proper are Europe and Africa: the ___E:Strait of Gibraltar U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strait_of_Gibraltar)___ (where it connects with the ___E:Mediterranean Sea U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mediterranean_Sea)___ — one of its ___E:marginal seas U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marginal_sea)___ — and, in turn, the ___E:Black Sea U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Sea)___ , both of which also touch upon Asia).
In the southeast, the Atlantic merges into the Indian Ocean.

The ___E:20° East meridian U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/20th_meridian_east)___ , running south from ___E:Cape Agulhas U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Agulhas)___ to ___E:Antarctica U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antarctica)___ defines its border.
In the 1953 definition it extends south to Antarctica, while in later maps it is bounded at the ___E:60° parallel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/60th_parallel_south)___ by the Southern Ocean.

The Atlantic has irregular coasts indented by numerous bays, gulfs and seas. These include the ___E:Baltic Sea U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltic_Sea)___ , ___E:Black Sea U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Sea)___ , ___E:Caribbean Sea U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribbean_Sea)___ , ___E:Davis Strait U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Davis_Strait)___ , ___E:Denmark Strait U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark_Strait)___ , part of the ___E:Drake Passage U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drake_Passage)___ , ___E:Gulf of Mexico U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_of_Mexico)___ , ___E:Labrador Sea U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labrador_Sea)___ , ___E:Mediterranean Sea U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mediterranean_Sea)___ , ___E:North Sea U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Sea)___ , ___E:Norwegian Sea U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norwegian_Sea)___ , almost all of the ___E:Scotia Sea U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotia_Sea)___ , and other tributary water bodies.
Including these marginal seas the coast line of the Atlantic measures 111,866 km (69,510 mi) compared to 135,663 km (84,297 mi) for the Pacific.

Including its marginal seas, the Atlantic covers an area of 106,460,000 km 2 (41,100,000 sq mi) or 23.5% of the global ocean and has a volume of 310,410,900 km 3 (74,471,500 cu mi) or 23.3% of the total volume of the Earth's oceans.
Excluding its marginal seas, the Atlantic covers 81,760,000 km 2 (31,570,000 sq mi) and has a volume of 305,811,900 km 3 (73,368,200 cu mi).
The North Atlantic covers 41,490,000 km 2 (16,020,000 sq mi) (11.5%) and the South Atlantic 40,270,000 km 2 (15,550,000 sq mi) (11.1%).

The average depth is 3,646 m (11,962 ft) and the maximum depth, the ___E:Milwaukee Deep U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milwaukee_Deep)___ in the ___E:Puerto Rico Trench U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puerto_Rico_Trench)___ , is 8,376 m (27,480 ft).

The ___E:bathymetry U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bathymetry)___ of the Atlantic is dominated by a ___E:submarine mountain range U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mid-ocean_ridge)___ called the ___E:Mid-Atlantic Ridge U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mid-Atlantic_Ridge)___ (MAR).

It runs from 87°N or 300 km (190 mi) south of the ___E:North Pole U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Pole)___ to the subantarctic ___E:Bouvet Island U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bouvet_Island)___ at ___E:54°S U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_parallel_south)___ .

Expeditions to explore the bathymertry of the Atlantic include the ___E:Challenger expedition U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger_expedition)___ and the ___E:German Meteor expedition U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_Meteor_expedition)___ ; as of 2001 [update] , ___E:Columbia University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_University)___ 's ___E:Lamont–Doherty Earth Observatory U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lamont%E2%80%93Doherty_Earth_Observatory)___ and the ___E:United States Navy Hydrographic Office U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Navy_Hydrographic_Office)___ conduct research on the ocean.
The MAR divides the Atlantic longitudinally into two halves, in each of which a series of basins are delimited by secondary, transverse ridges.

The MAR reaches above 2,000 m (6,600 ft) along most of its length, but is interrupted by larger transform faults at two places: the ___E:Romanche Trench U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanche_Trench)___ near the Equator and the ___E:Gibbs fracture zone U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gibbs_fracture_zone)___ at ___E:53°N U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/53rd_parallel_north)___ .
The MAR is a barrier for bottom water, but at these two transform faults deep water currents can pass from one side to the other.

The MAR rises 2–3 km (1.2–1.9 mi) above the surrounding ocean floor and its ___E:rift valley U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rift_valley)___ is the ___E:divergent boundary U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divergent_boundary)___ between the ___E:North American U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_American_plate)___ and ___E:Eurasian U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurasian_plate)___ plates in the North Atlantic and the ___E:South American U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_American_plate)___ and ___E:African U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_plate)___ plates in the South Atlantic.

The MAR produces ___E:basaltic volcanoes U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basaltic_lava)___ in ___E:Eyjafjallajökull U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eyjafjallaj%C3%B6kull)___ , Iceland, and ___E:pillow lava U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pillow_lava)___ on the ocean floor.

The depth of water at the apex of the ridge is less than 2,700 m (1,500 ___E:fathoms U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fathom)___ ; 8,900 ___E:ft U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foot_(unit))___ ) in most places, while the bottom of the ridge is three times as deep.

The MAR is intersected by two perpendicular ridges: the ___E:Azores–Gibraltar transform fault U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azores%E2%80%93Gibraltar_transform_fault)___ , the boundary between the ___E:Nubian U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nubian_plate)___ and ___E:Eurasian plates U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurasian_plate)___ , intersects the MAR at the ___E:Azores triple junction U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azores_triple_junction)___ , on either side of the Azores microplate, near the ___E:40°N U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/40th_parallel_north)___ .

A much vaguer, nameless boundary, between the North American and South American plates, intersects the MAR near or just north of the ___E:Fifteen-Twenty fracture zone U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fifteen-Twenty_fracture_zone)___ , approximately at ___E:16°N U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/16th_parallel_north)___ .
In the 1870s, the ___E:Challenger expedition U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger_expedition)___ discovered parts of what is now known as the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, or:

An elevated ridge rising to an average height of about 1,900 fathoms [3,500 m; 11,400 ft] below the surface traverses the basins of the North and South Atlantic in a meridianal direction from Cape Farewell, probably its far south at least as Gough Island, following roughly the outlines of the coasts of the Old and the New Worlds.
The remainder of the ridge was discovered in the 1920s by the ___E:German Meteor expedition U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_Meteor_expedition)___ using echo-sounding equipment.

The exploration of the MAR in the 1950s led to the general acceptance of ___E:seafloor spreading U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seafloor_spreading)___ and ___E:plate tectonics U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plate_tectonics)___ .
Most of the MAR runs under water but where it reaches the surfaces it has produced volcanic islands.

While nine of these have collectively been nominated a ___E:World Heritage Site U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Heritage_Site)___ for their geological value, four of them are considered of "Outstanding Universal Value" based on their cultural and natural criteria: ___E:Þingvellir U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%9Eingvellir_National_Park)___ , Iceland; ___E:Landscape of the Pico Island Vineyard Culture U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landscape_of_the_Pico_Island_Vineyard_Culture)___ , Portugal; ___E:Gough and Inaccessible Islands U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gough_and_Inaccessible_Islands)___ , United Kingdom; and Brazilian Atlantic Islands: ___E:Fernando de Noronha U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_de_Noronha)___ and ___E:Atol das Rocas U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atol_das_Rocas)___ Reserves, Brazil.
___E:Continental shelves U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continental_shelf)___ in the Atlantic are wide off Newfoundland, southernmost South America, and northeastern Europe.

In the western Atlantic ___E:carbonate platforms U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbonate_platform)___ dominate large areas, for example, the ___E:Blake Plateau U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blake_Plateau)___ and Bermuda Rise. The Atlantic is surrounded by ___E:passive margins U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passive_margin)___ except at a few locations where ___E:active margins U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Active_margin)___ form deep ___E:trenches U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oceanic_trench)___ : the ___E:Puerto Rico Trench U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puerto_Rico_Trench)___ (8,376 m or 27,480 ft maximum depth) in the western Atlantic and ___E:South Sandwich Trench U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Sandwich_Trench)___ (8,264 m or 27,113 ft) in the South Atlantic.
There are numerous submarine canyons off northeastern North America, western Europe, and northwestern Africa.
Some of these canyons extend along the continental rises and farther into the abyssal plains as deep-sea channels.
In 1922, a historic moment in cartography and oceanography occurred.
The USS Stewart used a Navy Sonic Depth Finder to draw a continuous map across the bed of the Atlantic.
This involved little guesswork because the idea of sonar is straightforward with pulses being sent from the vessel, which bounce off the ocean floor, then return to the vessel.

The deep ocean floor is thought to be fairly flat with occasional deeps, ___E:abyssal plains U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abyssal_plain)___ , ___E:trenches U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oceanic_trench)___ , ___E:seamounts U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seamount)___ , ___E:basins U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oceanic_basin)___ , ___E:plateaus U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oceanic_plateau)___ , ___E:canyons U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Submarine_canyon)___ , and some ___E:guyots U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guyot)___ .
Various shelves along the margins of the continents constitute about 11% of the bottom topography with few deep channels cut across the continental rise.

The mean depth between ___E:60°N U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/60th_parallel_north)___ and ___E:60°S U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/60th_parallel_south)___ is 3,730 m (12,240 ft), or close to the average for the global ocean, with a modal depth between 4,000 and 5,000 m (13,000 and 16,000 ft).

In the South Atlantic the ___E:Walvis Ridge U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walvis_Ridge)___ and ___E:Rio Grande Rise U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_Grande_Rise)___ form barriers to ocean currents.
The ___E:Laurentian Abyss U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurentian_Abyss)___ is found off the eastern coast of Canada.
Surface water temperatures, which vary with latitude, current systems, and season and reflect the latitudinal distribution of solar energy, range from below −2 °C (28 °F) to over 30 °C (86 °F).
Maximum temperatures occur north of the equator, and minimum values are found in the polar regions.
In the middle latitudes, the area of maximum temperature variations, values may vary by 7–8 °C (13–14 °F).

From October to June the surface is usually covered with sea ice in the ___E:Labrador Sea U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labrador_Sea)___ , ___E:Denmark Strait U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark_Strait)___ , and Baltic Sea.  [failed verification]
The ___E:Coriolis effect U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coriolis_effect)___ circulates North Atlantic water in a clockwise direction, whereas South Atlantic water circulates counter-clockwise.
The south ___E:tides U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tide)___ in the Atlantic Ocean are semi-diurnal; that is, two high tides occur every 24 lunar hours.

In latitudes above ___E:40° North U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/40th_parallel_north)___ some east–west oscillation, known as the ___E:North Atlantic oscillation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Atlantic_oscillation)___ , occurs.

On average, the Atlantic is the saltiest major ocean; surface water ___E:salinity U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salinity)___ in the open ocean ranges from 33 to 37 parts per thousand (3.3–3.7%) by mass and varies with latitude and season.
Evaporation, precipitation, river inflow and ___E:sea ice U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_ice)___ melting influence surface salinity values.

Although the lowest salinity values are just north of the equator (because of heavy tropical rainfall), in general, the lowest values are in the high latitudes and along coasts where large rivers enter.

Maximum salinity values occur at about ___E:25° north U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/25th_parallel_north)___ and ___E:south U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/25th_parallel_south)___ , in ___E:subtropical U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subtropical)___ regions with low rainfall and high evaporation.

The high surface salinity in the Atlantic, on which the Atlantic ___E:thermohaline circulation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermohaline_circulation)___ is dependent, is maintained by two processes: the ___E:Agulhas Leakage/Rings U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agulhas_Current#Agulhas_leakage_and_rings)___ , which brings salty Indian Ocean waters into the South Atlantic, and the "Atmospheric Bridge", which evaporates subtropical Atlantic waters and exports it to the Pacific.
The Atlantic Ocean consists of four major, upper ___E:water masses U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_mass)___ with distinct temperature and salinity.
The Atlantic subarctic upper water in the northernmost North Atlantic is the source for subarctic intermediate water and North Atlantic intermediate water.

North Atlantic central water can be divided into the eastern and western North Atlantic central water since the western part is strongly affected by the Gulf Stream and therefore the upper layer is closer to underlying fresher subpolar intermediate water.
The eastern water is saltier because of its proximity to Mediterranean water.
North Atlantic central water flows into South Atlantic central water at ___E:15°N U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/15th_parallel_north)___ .
There are five intermediate waters: four low-salinity waters formed at subpolar latitudes and one high-salinity formed through evaporation.

Arctic intermediate water flows from the north to become the source for North Atlantic deep water, south of the Greenland-Scotland sill. These two intermediate waters have different salinity in the western and eastern basins.

The wide range of salinities in the North Atlantic is caused by the asymmetry of the northern subtropical ___E:gyre U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gyre)___ and a large number of contributions from a wide range of sources: Labrador Sea, Norwegian-Greenland Sea, Mediterranean, and South Atlantic Intermediate Water.

The ___E:North Atlantic deep water U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Atlantic_Deep_Water)___ (NADW) is a complex of four water masses, two that form by deep convection in the open ocean – classical and upper Labrador sea water – and two that form from the inflow of dense water across the Greenland-Iceland-Scotland sill – Denmark Strait and Iceland-Scotland overflow water.

Along its path across Earth the composition of the NADW is affected by other water masses, especially ___E:Antarctic bottom water U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antarctic_Bottom_Water)___ and Mediterranean overflow water.
The NADW is fed by a flow of warm shallow water into the northern North Atlantic which is responsible for the anomalous warm climate in Europe.

Changes in the formation of NADW have been linked to global climate changes in the past. Since human-made substances were introduced into the environment, the path of the NADW can be traced throughout its course by measuring tritium and radiocarbon from ___E:nuclear weapon tests U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_weapon_test)___ in the 1960s and ___E:CFCs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chlorofluorocarbon)___ .

The clockwise warm-water ___E:North Atlantic Gyre U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Atlantic_Gyre)___ occupies the northern Atlantic, and the counter-clockwise warm-water ___E:South Atlantic Gyre U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Atlantic_Gyre)___ appears in the southern Atlantic.

In the North Atlantic, surface circulation is dominated by three inter-connected currents: the ___E:Gulf Stream U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_Stream)___ which flows north-east from the North American coast at ___E:Cape Hatteras U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Hatteras)___ ; the ___E:North Atlantic Current U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Atlantic_Current)___ , a branch of the Gulf Stream which flows northward from the ___E:Grand Banks U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Banks_of_Newfoundland)___ ; and the ___E:Subpolar Front U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Subpolar_Front&action=edit&redlink=1)___ , an extension of the North Atlantic Current, a wide, vaguely defined region separating the subtropical gyre from the subpolar gyre. This system of currents transports warm water into the North Atlantic, without which temperatures in the North Atlantic and Europe would plunge dramatically.

North of the North Atlantic Gyre, the cyclonic ___E:North Atlantic Subpolar Gyre U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=North_Atlantic_Subpolar_Gyre&action=edit&redlink=1)___ plays a key role in climate variability.
It is governed by ocean currents from marginal seas and regional topography, rather than being steered by wind, both in the deep ocean and at sea level.
The subpolar gyre forms an important part of the global ___E:thermohaline circulation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermohaline_circulation)___ .

Its eastern portion includes ___E:eddying U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_(fluid_dynamics))___ branches of the ___E:North Atlantic Current U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Atlantic_Current)___ which transport warm, saline waters from the subtropics to the northeastern Atlantic.

There this water is cooled during winter and forms return currents that merge along the eastern continental slope of Greenland where they form an intense (40–50 ___E:Sv U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sverdrup)___ ) current which flows around the continental margins of the ___E:Labrador Sea U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labrador_Sea)___ .
A third of this water becomes part of the deep portion of the ___E:North Atlantic Deep Water U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Atlantic_Deep_Water)___ (NADW).

The NADW, in turn, feeds the ___E:meridional overturning circulation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meridional_overturning_circulation)___ (MOC), the northward heat transport of which is threatened by anthropogenic climate change.

Large variations in the subpolar gyre on a decade-century scale, associated with the ___E:North Atlantic oscillation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Atlantic_oscillation)___ , are especially pronounced in ___E:Labrador Sea Water U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labrador_Sea_Water)___ , the upper layers of the MOC.

The South Atlantic is dominated by the anti-cyclonic southern subtropical gyre. The ___E:South Atlantic Central Water U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=South_Atlantic_Central_Water&action=edit&redlink=1)___ originates in this gyre, while ___E:Antarctic Intermediate Water U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antarctic_Intermediate_Water)___ originates in the upper layers of the circumpolar region, near the ___E:Drake Passage U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drake_Passage)___ and the Falkland Islands.
Both these currents receive some contribution from the Indian Ocean.

On the African east coast, the small cyclonic ___E:Angola Gyre U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Angola_Gyre&action=edit&redlink=1)___ lies embedded in the large subtropical gyre.  The southern subtropical gyre is partly masked by a wind-induced ___E:Ekman layer U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ekman_layer)___ .

The residence time of the gyre is 4.4–8.5 years. ___E:North Atlantic Deep Water U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Atlantic_Deep_Water)___ flows southward below the ___E:thermocline U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermocline)___ of the subtropical gyre.

The Sargasso Sea in the western North Atlantic can be defined as the area where two species of Sargassum ( S. fluitans and natans ) float, an area 4,000 km (2,500 mi) wide and encircled by the ___E:Gulf Stream U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_Stream)___ , ___E:North Atlantic Drift U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Atlantic_Drift)___ , and ___E:North Equatorial Current U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Equatorial_Current)___ .

This population of seaweed probably originated from Tertiary ancestors on the European shores of the former ___E:Tethys Ocean U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tethys_Ocean)___ and has, if so, maintained itself by ___E:vegetative growth U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vegetative_reproduction)___ , floating in the ocean for millions of years.

Other species endemic to the Sargasso Sea include the ___E:sargassum fish U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sargassum_fish)___ , a predator with algae-like appendages which hovers motionless among the Sargassum .

Fossils of similar fishes have been found in fossil bays of the former Tethys Ocean, in what is now the ___E:Carpathian U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carpathian_Mountains)___ region, that were similar to the Sargasso Sea. It is possible that the population in the Sargasso Sea migrated to the Atlantic as the Tethys closed at the end of the Miocene around 17 Ma.  The origin of the Sargasso fauna and flora remained enigmatic for centuries.

The fossils found in the Carpathians in the mid-20th century often called the "quasi-Sargasso assemblage", finally showed that this assemblage originated in the ___E:Carpathian Basin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carpathian_Basin)___ from where it migrated over ___E:Sicily U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sicily)___ to the central Atlantic where it evolved into modern species of the Sargasso Sea.

The location of the spawning ground for ___E:European eels U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_eel)___ ___E:remained unknown for decades U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eel_life_history#Search_for_the_spawning_grounds)___ .

In the early 19th century it was discovered that the southern Sargasso Sea is the spawning ground for both the ___E:European U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_eel)___ and ___E:American eel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_eel)___ and that the former migrate more than 5,000 km (3,100 mi) and the latter 2,000 km (1,200 mi).
Ocean currents such as the Gulf Stream transport eel larvae from the Sargasso Sea to foraging areas in North America, Europe, and northern Africa.

Recent but disputed research suggests that eels possibly use ___E:Earth's magnetic field U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth%27s_magnetic_field)___ to navigate through the ocean both as larvae and as adults.
The climate is influenced by the temperatures of the surface waters and water currents as well as winds.

Because of the ocean's great capacity to store and release heat, maritime climates are more moderate and have less extreme seasonal variations than inland climates. ___E:Precipitation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Precipitation_(meteorology))___ can be approximated from coastal weather data and air temperature from water temperatures.
The oceans are the major source of atmospheric moisture that is obtained through evaporation.
Climatic zones vary with latitude; the warmest zones stretch across the Atlantic north of the equator.

The coldest zones are in high latitudes, with the coldest regions corresponding to the areas covered by sea ice. Ocean currents influence the climate by transporting warm and cold waters to other regions.
The winds that are cooled or warmed when blowing over these currents influence adjacent land areas.

The ___E:Gulf Stream U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_Stream)___ and its northern extension towards Europe, the ___E:North Atlantic Drift U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Atlantic_Current)___ is thought to have at least some influence on climate.
For example, the Gulf Stream helps moderate winter temperatures along the coastline of southeastern North America, keeping it warmer in winter along the coast than inland areas.
The Gulf Stream also keeps extreme temperatures from occurring on the Florida Peninsula.

In the higher latitudes, the North Atlantic Drift, warms the atmosphere over the oceans, keeping the British Isles and northwestern Europe mild and cloudy, and not severely cold in winter, like other locations at the same high latitude.

The cold water currents contribute to heavy fog off the coast of eastern Canada (the ___E:Grand Banks of Newfoundland U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Banks_of_Newfoundland)___ area) and Africa's northwestern coast.
In general, winds transport moisture and air over land areas.

Every winter, the ___E:Icelandic Low U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Icelandic_Low)___ produces frequent storms. ___E:Icebergs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceberg)___ are common from early February to the end of July across the shipping lanes near the ___E:Grand Banks of Newfoundland U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Banks_of_Newfoundland)___ .
The ice season is longer in the polar regions, but there is little shipping in those areas.
___E:Hurricanes U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_hurricane)___ are a hazard in the western parts of the North Atlantic during the summer and autumn.

Due to a consistently strong ___E:wind shear U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wind_shear)___ and a weak ___E:Intertropical Convergence Zone U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intertropical_Convergence_Zone)___ , ___E:South Atlantic tropical cyclones U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Atlantic_tropical_cyclone)___ are rare.

The Atlantic Ocean is underlain mostly by dense ___E:mafic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mafic)___ oceanic crust made up of ___E:basalt U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basalt)___ and ___E:gabbro U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabbro)___ and overlain by fine clay, silt and siliceous ooze on the abyssal plain.

The continental margins and continental shelf mark lower density, but greater thickness ___E:felsic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felsic)___ continental rock that is often much older than that of the seafloor.
The oldest oceanic crust in the Atlantic is up to 145 million years and is situated off the west coast of Africa and the east coast of North America, or on either side of the South Atlantic.
In many places, the continental shelf and continental slope are covered in thick sedimentary layers.

For instance, on the North American side of the ocean, large carbonate deposits formed in warm shallow waters such as Florida and the Bahamas, while coarse river outwash sands and silt are common in shallow shelf areas like the ___E:Georges Bank U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Bank)___ .

Coarse sand, boulders, and rocks were transported into some areas, such as off the coast of Nova Scotia or the ___E:Gulf of Maine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_of_Maine)___ during the ___E:Pleistocene U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pleistocene)___ ice ages.

The break-up of ___E:Pangaea U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pangaea)___ began in the central Atlantic, between North America and Northwest Africa, where rift basins opened during the Late Triassic and Early Jurassic.
This period also saw the first stages of the uplift of the Atlas Mountains.
The exact timing is controversial with estimates ranging from 200 to 170 Ma.

The opening of the Atlantic Ocean coincided with the initial break-up of the supercontinent ___E:Pangaea U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pangaea)___ , both of which were initiated by the eruption of the ___E:Central Atlantic Magmatic Province U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Atlantic_Magmatic_Province)___ (CAMP), one of the most extensive and voluminous ___E:large igneous provinces U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Large_igneous_province)___ in Earth's history associated with the ___E:Triassic–Jurassic extinction event U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triassic%E2%80%93Jurassic_extinction_event)___ , one of Earth's major ___E:extinction events U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extinction_event)___ .

Theoliitic ___E:dikes U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dike_(geology))___ , ___E:sills U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aquatic_sill)___ , and lava flows from the CAMP eruption at 200 Ma have been found in West Africa, eastern North America, and northern South America.
The extent of the volcanism has been estimated to 4.5 × 10 6 km 2 (1.7 × 10 6 sq mi) of which 2.5 × 10 6 km 2 (9.7 × 10 5 sq mi) covered what is now northern and central Brazil.

The formation of the ___E:Central American Isthmus U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_American_Isthmus)___ closed the ___E:Central American Seaway U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_American_Seaway)___ at the end of the Pliocene 2.8 Ma ago. The formation of the isthmus resulted in the migration and extinction of many land-living animals, known as the ___E:Great American Interchange U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_American_Interchange)___ , but the closure of the seaway resulted in a "Great American Schism" as it affected ocean currents, salinity, and temperatures in both the Atlantic and Pacific.
Marine organisms on both sides of the isthmus became isolated and either diverged or went extinct.

Geologically, the North Atlantic is the area delimited to the south by two conjugate margins, Newfoundland and Iberia, and to the north by the Arctic ___E:Eurasian Basin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurasian_Basin)___ .

The opening of the North Atlantic closely followed the margins of its predecessor, the ___E:Iapetus Ocean U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iapetus_Ocean)___ , and spread from the central Atlantic in six stages: ___E:Iberia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iberian_Peninsula)___ – ___E:Newfoundland U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newfoundland_(island))___ , ___E:Porcupine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porcupine_Bank)___ –North America, Eurasia–Greenland, Eurasia–North America.
Active and inactive spreading systems in this area are marked by the interaction with the ___E:Iceland hotspot U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland_hotspot)___ .
Seafloor spreading led to the extension of the crust and the formation of troughs and sedimentary basins.
The Rockall Trough opened between 105 and 84 million years ago although the rift failed along with one leading into the ___E:Bay of Biscay U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay_of_Biscay)___ .

Spreading began opening the ___E:Labrador Sea U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labrador_Sea)___ around 61 million years ago, continuing until 36 million years ago. Geologists distinguish two magmatic phases.
One from 62 to 58 million years ago predates the separation of Greenland from northern Europe while the second from 56 to 52 million years ago happened as the separation occurred.
___E:Iceland U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland_Plateau)___ began to form 62 million years ago due to a particularly concentrated mantle plume.

Large quantities of ___E:basalt U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basalt)___ erupted at this time period are found on Baffin Island, Greenland, the Faroe Islands, and Scotland, with ash falls in Western Europe acting as a stratigraphic marker.
The opening of the North Atlantic caused a significant uplift of continental crust along the coast.

For instance, despite 7 km thick basalt, Gunnbjorn Field in East Greenland is the highest point on the island, elevated enough that it exposes older Mesozoic sedimentary rocks at its base, similar to old lava fields above sedimentary rocks in the uplifted Hebrides of western Scotland.
The North Atlantic Ocean contains about 810 ___E:seamounts U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seamount)___ , most of them situated along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

The ___E:OSPAR U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OSPAR_Convention)___ database (Convention for the Protection of the Marine Environment of the North-East Atlantic) mentions 104 seamounts: 74 within national ___E:exclusive economic zones U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exclusive_economic_zone)___ .
Of these seamounts, 46 are located close to the ___E:Iberian Peninsula U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iberian_Peninsula)___ .
West Gondwana (South America and Africa) broke up in the Early Cretaceous to form the South Atlantic.

The apparent fit between the coastlines of the two continents was noted on the first maps that included the South Atlantic and it was also the subject of the first computer-assisted plate tectonic reconstructions in 1965.   This magnificent fit, however, has since then proven problematic and later reconstructions have introduced various deformation zones along the shorelines to accommodate the northward-propagating break-up.  Intra-continental rifts and deformations have also been introduced to subdivide both continental plates into sub-plates.

Geologically, the South Atlantic can be divided into four segments: equatorial segment, from 10°N to the Romanche fracture zone (RFZ); central segment, from RFZ to Florianopolis fracture zone (FFZ, north of Walvis Ridge and Rio Grande Rise); southern segment, from FFZ to the Agulhas–Falkland fracture zone (AFFZ); and Falkland segment, south of AFFZ.

In the southern segment the Early Cretaceous (133–130 Ma) intensive ___E:magmatism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magmatism)___ of the ___E:Paraná–Etendeka Large Igneous Province U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paran%C3%A1_and_Etendeka_traps)___ produced by the ___E:Tristan hotspot U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tristan_hotspot)___ resulted in an estimated volume of 1.5 × 10 6 to 2.0 × 10 6 km 3 (3.6 × 10 5 to 4.8 × 10 5 cu mi).

It covered an area of 1.2 × 10 6 to 1.6 × 10 6 km 2 (4.6 × 10 5 to 6.2 × 10 5 sq mi) in Brazil, Paraguay, and Uruguay and 0.8 × 10 5 km 2 (3.1 × 10 4 sq mi) in Africa. ___E:Dyke swarms U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dyke_swarm)___ in Brazil, Angola, eastern Paraguay, and Namibia, however, suggest the LIP originally covered a much larger area and also indicate failed rifts in all these areas.
Associated offshore basaltic flows reach as far south as the Falkland Islands and South Africa.
Traces of magmatism in both offshore and onshore basins in the central and southern segments have been dated to 147–49 Ma with two peaks between 143 and 121 Ma and 90–60 Ma.
In the Falkland segment rifting began with dextral movements between the Patagonia and Colorado sub-plates between the Early Jurassic (190 Ma) and the Early Cretaceous (126.7 Ma).
Around 150 Ma sea-floor spreading propagated northward into the southern segment.
No later than 130 Ma rifting had reached the Walvis Ridge–Rio Grande Rise.

In the central segment, rifting started to break Africa in two by opening the ___E:Benue Trough U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benue_Trough)___ around 118 Ma. Rifting in the central segment, however, coincided with the ___E:Cretaceous Normal Superchron U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geomagnetic_reversal#Superchrons)___ (also known as the Cretaceous quiet period), a 40 Ma period without magnetic reversals, which makes it difficult to date sea-floor spreading in this segment.
The equatorial segment is the last phase of the break-up, but, because it is located on the Equator, magnetic anomalies cannot be used for dating.

Various estimates date the propagation of seafloor spreading in this segment and consequent opening of the Equatorial Atlantic Gateway (EAG) to the period 120–96 Ma.   This final stage, nevertheless, coincided with or resulted in the end of continental extension in Africa.

About 50 Ma the opening of the ___E:Drake Passage U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drake_Passage)___ resulted from a change in the motions and separation rate of the South American and Antarctic plates.

First, small ocean basins opened and a shallow gateway appeared during the Middle Eocene. 34–30 Ma a deeper seaway developed, followed by an ___E:Eocene–Oligocene climatic deterioration U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eocene%E2%80%93Oligocene_extinction_event)___ and the growth of the ___E:Antarctic ice sheet U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antarctic_ice_sheet)___ .
An embryonic subduction margin is potentially developing west of Gibraltar.

The ___E:Gibraltar Arc U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gibraltar_Arc)___ in the western Mediterranean is migrating westward into the central Atlantic where it joins the converging African and Eurasian plates.
Together these three tectonic forces are slowly developing into a new subduction system in the eastern Atlantic Basin.

Meanwhile, the ___E:Scotia Arc U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotia_Arc)___ and ___E:Caribbean plate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribbean_plate)___ in the western Atlantic Basin are eastward-propagating subduction systems that might, together with the Gibraltar system, represent the beginning of the closure of the Atlantic Ocean and the final stage of the Atlantic ___E:Wilson cycle U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_cycle)___ .

___E:Mitochondrial DNA U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitochondrial_DNA)___ (mtDNA) studies indicate that 80,000–60,000 years ago a major demographic expansion within Africa, derived from a single, small population, coincided with the emergence of behavioral complexity and the rapid ___E:MIS U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_isotope_stage)___ 5–4 environmental changes.

This group of people not only expanded over the whole of Africa, but also started to disperse ___E:out of Africa U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recent_African_origin_of_modern_humans)___ into Asia, Europe, and Australasia around 65,000 years ago and quickly replaced the archaic humans in these regions.

During the ___E:Last Glacial Maximum U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Last_Glacial_Maximum)___ (LGM) 20,000 years ago humans had to abandon their initial settlements along the European North Atlantic coast and retreat to the Mediterranean.
Following rapid climate changes at the end of the LGM this region was repopulated by ___E:Magdalenian U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magdalenian)___ culture.

Other hunter-gatherers followed in waves interrupted by hazards such as the ___E:Laacher See U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laacher_See)___ volcanic eruption, the inundation of ___E:Doggerland U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doggerland)___ (now the ___E:North Sea U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Sea)___ ), and the formation of the ___E:Baltic Sea U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltic_Sea)___ .
The European coasts of the North Atlantic were permanently populated about 9,000–8.5,000 years ago.

This human dispersal left abundant traces along the coasts of the Atlantic Ocean. 50 kya-old, deeply stratified ___E:shell middens U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shell_midden)___ found in ___E:Ysterfontein U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ysterfontein)___ on the western coast of South Africa are associated with the Middle Stone Age (MSA).
The MSA population was small and dispersed and the rate of their reproduction and exploitation was less intense than those of later generations.

While their middens resemble 12–11 kya-old Late Stone Age (LSA) middens found on every inhabited continent, the 50–45 kya-old ___E:Enkapune Ya Muto U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enkapune_Ya_Muto)___ in Kenya probably represents the oldest traces of the first modern humans to disperse out of Africa.
The same development can be seen in Europe.

In ___E:La Riera Cave U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=La_Riera_Cave&action=edit&redlink=1)___ (23–13 kya) in Asturias, Spain, only some 26,600 molluscs were deposited over 10 kya. In contrast, 8–7 kya-old shell middens in Portugal, Denmark, and Brazil generated thousands of tons of debris and artefacts.

The ___E:Ertebølle U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erteb%C3%B8lle_culture)___ middens in Denmark, for example, accumulated 2,000 m 3 (71,000 cu ft) of shell deposits representing some 50 million molluscs over only a thousand years.

This intensification in the exploitation of marine resources has been described as accompanied by new technologies – such as boats, harpoons, and fish hooks – because many caves found in the Mediterranean and on the European Atlantic coast have increased quantities of marine shells in their upper levels and reduced quantities in their lower.
The earliest exploitation took place on the submerged shelves, now submerged and most settlements now excavated were then located several kilometers from these shelves.
The reduced quantities of shells in the lower levels can represent the few shells that were exported inland.

During the LGM the ___E:Laurentide Ice Sheet U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurentide_Ice_Sheet)___ covered most of northern North America while ___E:Beringia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beringia)___ connected Siberia to Alaska.

In 1973, late American geoscientist ___E:Paul S. Martin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Schultz_Martin)___ proposed a "blitzkrieg" colonization of the Americas by which ___E:Clovis hunters U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clovis_culture)___ migrated into North America around 13,000 years ago in a single wave through an ice-free corridor in the ice sheet and "spread southward explosively, briefly attaining a density sufficiently large to overkill much of their prey."  Others later proposed a "three-wave" migration over the ___E:Bering Land Bridge U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bering_Land_Bridge)___ .

These hypotheses remained the long-held view regarding the ___E:settlement of the Americas U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prehistoric_migration_and_settlement_of_the_Americas_from_Asia)___ , a view challenged by more recent archaeological discoveries: the oldest archaeological sites in the Americas have been found in South America; sites in northeast Siberia report virtually no human presence there during the LGM; and most Clovis artefacts have been found in eastern North America along the Atlantic coast.

Furthermore, colonisation models based on mtDNA, ___E:yDNA U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YDNA)___ , and ___E:atDNA U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AtDNA)___ data respectively support neither the "blitzkrieg" nor the "three-wave" hypotheses but they also deliver mutually ambiguous results.
Contradictory data from archaeology and genetics will most likely deliver future hypotheses that will, eventually, confirm each other.

A proposed route across the Pacific to South America could explain early South American finds and another hypothesis proposes a northern path, through the Canadian Arctic and down the North American Atlantic coast.

Early settlements across the Atlantic have been suggested by alternative theories, ranging from purely hypothetical to mostly disputed, including the ___E:Solutrean hypothesis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solutrean_hypothesis)___ and some of the ___E:Pre-Columbian trans-oceanic contact theories U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pre-Columbian_trans-oceanic_contact_theories)___ .

The ___E:Norse settlement U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norse_colonization_of_North_America)___ of the ___E:Faroe Islands U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faroe_Islands)___ and ___E:Iceland U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland)___ began during the 9th and 10th centuries.

A settlement on ___E:Greenland U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenland)___ was established before 1000 CE, but contact with it was lost in 1409 and it was finally abandoned during the early ___E:Little Ice Age U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Ice_Age)___ .

This setback was caused by a range of factors: an unsustainable economy resulted in erosion and denudation, while conflicts with the local ___E:Inuit U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inuit)___ resulted in the failure to adapt their Arctic technologies; a colder climate resulted in starvation, and the colony got economically marginalized as the ___E:Great Plague U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Plague)___ harvested its victims on Iceland in the 15th century.
Iceland was initially settled 865–930 CE following a warm period when winter temperatures hovered around 2 °C (36 °F) which made farming favorable at high latitudes.
This did not last, however, and temperatures quickly dropped; at 1080 CE summer temperatures had reached a maximum of 5 °C (41 °F).

The Landnámabók ( Book of Settlement ) records disastrous famines during the first century of settlement – "men ate foxes and ravens" and "the old and helpless were killed and thrown over cliffs" – and by the early 1200s hay had to be abandoned for short-season crops such as ___E:barley U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barley)___ .

___E:Christopher Columbus U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Columbus)___ ___E:reached the Americas U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voyages_of_Christopher_Columbus)___ in 1492, sailing under the Spanish flag.  Six years later ___E:Vasco da Gama U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasco_da_Gama)___ reached India under the Portuguese flag, by navigating south around the ___E:Cape of Good Hope U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_of_Good_Hope)___ , thus proving that the Atlantic and Indian Oceans are connected.

In 1500, in his voyage to India following Vasco da Gama, ___E:Pedro Álvares Cabral U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pedro_%C3%81lvares_Cabral)___ reached Brazil, taken by the currents of the ___E:South Atlantic Gyre U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Atlantic_Gyre)___ .

Following these explorations, Spain and Portugal quickly ___E:conquered and colonized U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonization_of_the_Americas)___ large territories in the New World and forced the Amerindian population into slavery in order to exploit the vast quantities of silver and gold they found.

Spain and Portugal monopolized this trade in order to keep other European nations out, but conflicting interests nevertheless led to a series of Spanish-Portuguese wars. A peace treaty mediated by the Pope divided the conquered territories into Spanish and Portuguese sectors while keeping other colonial powers away. England, France, and the Dutch Republic enviously watched the Spanish and Portuguese wealth grow and allied themselves with ___E:pirates U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piracy_in_the_Atlantic_World)___ such as ___E:Henry Mainwaring U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Mainwaring)___ and ___E:Alexandre Exquemelin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandre_Exquemelin)___ .
They could explore the convoys leaving the Americas because prevailing winds and currents made the transport of heavy metals slow and predictable.
